title: The heavens torn open (Mark 1:9–13)
hook: the sky rips, the Spirit comes down like a dove, then straight into the desert

segments.voice: Yesterday: gospel, good news, and a man in camel hair by the Jordan. Your line was the beginning of the good news.

John said someone mightier was coming. Now he arrives, and Mark gives him no introduction at all. No backstory, no childhood. Just: in those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. One sentence. He walks down into the river with everyone else. Then he comes up out of the water, and Mark describes what happens with a word so violent it's almost shocking. Not the sky opening politely, like curtains. The sky ripping. And before you've even caught your breath, it's over, and he's alone in the desert. Five verses.
screen: `NO BACKSTORY, ONE SENTENCE.` → `INTO THE RIVER WITH EVERYONE.` → `THE SKY RIPS.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible says it gently: "And straightway coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit like a dove descending upon him." But Mark's Greek word is schizō: to tear, to split, to rip. It's the root of the English word schism. Matthew and Luke, telling the same scene, use the ordinary word for open. Mark says torn. And the verb comes back at the very end of Mark: when Jesus dies on the cross, the curtain of the Temple is torn in two from top to bottom. Same word, beginning and end, framing the whole story: heaven ripped open to earth. Then a voice: "Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Notice when it comes. Before a single miracle. Before a sermon. Before he's done anything at all. Beloved first. Then, right away, the turn: "And immediately the spirit driveth him into the wilderness." Driveth is a strong word, the one Mark later uses for casting out demons. The Spirit that came down like a dove now drives him out. Forty days in the wilderness, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, and angels serving him. Mark gives none of the conversation with the tempter that Matthew and Luke tell. Just wild animals and angels, side by side. Some readers take comfort from the order: being beloved doesn't mean skipping the desert. In Mark, the voice comes first.
screen: `SCHIZŌ — THE SKY RIPS.` · `TORN AT THE START, TORN AT THE CROSS.` · `BELOVED, BEFORE HE'D DONE ANYTHING.` · `DRIVEN INTO THE WILDERNESS.` · then, large: `THOU ART MY BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: Slow Mark down: picture the water, then coming up out of it. If you're a Christian, you might hear the voice as spoken to you too, through baptism: beloved; if you're not, simply notice what it would mean to be loved before you've done anything. Then think about the desert you're walking into this week, and let the first word go with you into it.
Schizō, Mark's violent word for tear or rip: the heavens torn open at his baptism, and the Temple curtain torn at his death.
Your line: beloved, then the desert. The dove and the driving come from the same Spirit. Day one hundred fifty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Many churches remember Jesus's baptism at the feast of the Baptism of the Lord or Theophany in January, and some lectionaries read Mark's desert verses at the start of Lent, when a season of forty days begins.

original.note: Greek: being torn apart — Mark's word for the heavens (1:10); schism comes from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: the sky opened and a dove came down.
what it means: the sky ripped, a voice said beloved, and the Spirit drove him straight into the desert.
what a scholar hears: schizomenous in 1:10 and eschisthē in 15:38 (the Temple veil) bracket Mark's gospel; Matthew and Luke soften it to opened.
recall: telling plainly what you saw happen to you

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'only one other time' count softened (Mark 2:21 has the related noun schisma); stock line 'Christians have found comfort here for centuries' and the narrator's own theological claim reframed as what some readers take; howItsDone lectionary claim hedged.

Mark 1:10 σχιζομένους vs Matthew 3:16 and Luke 3:21 (ἀνοίγω, opened). Mark 15:38 ἐσχίσθη. 'Only one other time in his gospel': the verb schizō appears in Mark at 1:10 and 15:38; Mark 2:21 has the related noun schisma (a tear in cloth). Confirm the claim is limited to the verb.
Driveth: ἐκβάλλει, the verb Mark also uses for casting out demons. Confirm.
Practice links 'beloved' to baptism for Christians; kept as an invitation. Confirm.
howItsDone: the Baptism of the Lord (Western) / Theophany (Orthodox, January 6); Mark 1:9–15 is read on the First Sunday of Lent in Year B of the Revised Common and Catholic lectionaries. Confirm.
